en: The Haṭhayoga-pradīpikā (1) First Instruction:
Homage be to that venerable Ādinātha.
The science of Haṭhayoga, taught by him,
shines like a staircase for one who desires to ascend to the exalted Royal Yoga (Rājayoga). (HYP 1.1)
Having bowed to the venerable Guru, the Lord, the yogi Svātmārāma teaches the science of Haṭha solely for the sake of Rāja-yoga. (HYP 1.2)
To those who, due to delusion, are shrouded in the great darkness of ignorance regarding Rājayoga, Svātmārāma, the compassionate one, offers this *Haṭhapradīpikā*. (HYP 1.3)
Indeed, Matsyendra, Gorakṣa, and others know this science of Haṭha;
or else, a yogi who delights in his own self knows it through their grace. (HYP 1.4)
Śrī Ādinātha, Matsyendra, Śāvarānanda, and Bhairava; Cauraṅgī, Mīna, Gorakṣa, Virūpākṣa, and Bileśaya.
Manthāna, Bhairava, Yogī, Siddhi, Buddha, Kanthaḍi,
Koraṇṭaka, Surānanda, Siddhapāda, and Carpaṭi.
Kānerī, Pūjyapāda, Nityanātha, Nirañjana, Kapālī, Bindunātha, and the one named Kākacaṇḍīśvara.
Allāma, Prabhudeva, Ghoḍā, Colī,
Ṭiṃṭiṇi, Bhānukī, Nāradeva, Khaṇḍa, and likewise Kāpālika.
These and other great adepts, by the power of haṭhayoga,
having shattered the rod of Time, wander throughout the universe.
For those scorched by the heat of all sufferings, Haṭha is the refuge-monastery;
for those engaged in all forms of yoga, Haṭha is the supporting tortoise.
The science of Haṭha must be kept strictly secret by the yogi who desires accomplishment;
it becomes powerful when concealed, but powerless when revealed. (HYP 1.11)
In a well-governed, righteous country, where food is abundant and there is no affliction,
within a distance of one bow-length, free from stones, fire, and water,
the practitioner of *haṭhayoga* should reside in the middle of a small hut in a secluded spot. (HYP 1.12)
With few doors, free from cracks, pits, or holes, neither too high nor too low in height, well-smeared with thick cow dung, stainless, and cleared of all living beings;
its exterior made beautiful by pavilions, altars, and wells, and surrounded by a wall.
This definition of a yoga monastery has been proclaimed by the perfected ones who practice Haṭha.
Staying in such a hermitage, free from all anxieties,
one should practice yoga alone according to the path taught by the guru.
Excessive eating, overexertion, excessive talk, obsession with rules, attachment to people, and fickleness— by these six, yoga is destroyed.
Through enthusiasm, daring, fortitude, the knowledge of reality, certainty,
and the renunciation of association with worldly people— by these six, yoga is perfected.

Now, as for the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas): non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, forbearance, fortitude, compassion, straightforwardness, moderation in diet, and purity—these are the ten restraints. (HYP 1.17)
Austerity, contentment, faith, charity, worship of the Lord,
listening to the words of the established doctrine, modesty, and the offering of oblations—
these ten are proclaimed as the observances (niyamas) by those proficient in the Yoga scriptures. (HYP 1.18)
Now, since posture (*āsana*) is the first limb of *haṭha*, posture is described first:
"One should practice that posture which brings stability, health, and lightness of the limbs" (HYP 1.19).
I shall now describe some of the postures (āsanas) adopted by sages such as Vasiṣṭha and others, and by yogins such as Matsyendra and others. (HYP 1.20)
Having properly placed both soles of the feet between the knees and the thighs,
sitting with the body straight— this they call the *svastika* posture.
One should place the right ankle on the left side of the back, and likewise the left ankle on the right; this posture, shaped like a cow's face, is called Gomukha.
One should place one foot firmly upon the opposite thigh, and likewise the other thigh upon its corresponding foot; this is called *vīrāsana*.
Restraining the anus with the two heels in reverse order, one who is concentrated—this is known as the tortoise posture (kūrmāsana) by those who know yoga. (HYP 1.24)
Having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), with the hands placed between the knees and the thighs and resting on the ground, one establishes the cock posture (kukkuṭāsana) situated in space.
Seated in the cock-posture (kukkuṭāsana) and binding the neck with both arms, one should lie flat on the back like a tortoise;
this is the "Supine Tortoise" (uttāna-kūrmaka).
Grasping the two big toes with the hands up to the ears, one should perform the drawing of the bow; this is called the bow posture (dhanurāsana).
Placing the right foot at the base of the left thigh and wrapping the left foot around the outside of the knee,
one should stand with the body turned.
The posture taught by the venerable Matsyendranātha is as follows. HYP 1.28.
The seat of Matsyendra, the radiance of the stomach,
the weapon that shatters the mandala of fierce disease,
and the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī through practice.
And it bestows stability upon the moon for men.
Having stretched out his two legs on the ground like staffs and grasped the tips of both feet with his two arms,
he placed the region of his forehead upon his knees.
They say this is the final resting place.
Thus, this supreme posture, the *paścimatāna*,
causes the vital wind to flow toward the rear and brings about the rising of the digestive fire within the belly.
It brings about leanness of the abdomen and freedom from disease for men.
Supporting the earth with both hands, with his elbows placed at the sides of the navel,
he stands upon a high seat in the sky like a staff.
They declare this to be the Māyūra Pīṭha.
The Śrīmayūra posture quickly removes all diseases such as abdominal tumors and enlargement of the abdomen, overcomes the humors (doṣas),
and reduces even a large amount of poorly digested food to ashes entirely.
It generates the digestive fire and would digest even *kālakūṭa* poison.
Lying supine upon the ground like a corpse is the "corpse posture" (śavāsana);
it removes fatigue and brings rest to the mind. (HYP 1.34)
Eighty-four postures have been taught by Śiva;
taking from among them a quartet that constitutes the essence, I shall now describe them.
The fourfold group consisting of the Siddha, Padma, Siṃha, and Bhadra postures—among these, the Siddha posture is the most excellent; one should always remain in it for the sake of happiness.
Now, regarding Siddhāsana:
having firmly placed the root of one foot joined at the perineum (yoni-sthāna),
and having fixed the chin steadily against the heart, one should place the other foot upon the [opposite] thigh.
Standing like a pillar with senses restrained, one should gaze at the space between the eyebrows with a steady vision;
this is indeed called Siddhāsana, which effects the breaking open of the door to liberation.
Having placed the left ankle above the perineum,
and likewise having set the other ankle upon it, this shall be the Siddhāsana.
Some call this Siddhāsana; others know it as Vajrāsana. Some speak of it as Muktāsana, while others call it Guptāsana. (HYP 1.39)

Just as moderation in food is primary among the restraints (yamas), and non-violence among the observances (niyamas), the perfected ones know Siddhāsana to be the one foremost among all postures. HYP 1.40.
One should constantly practice that which is perfected in the eighty-four pīṭhas;
it is the purification of the impurities of the seventy-two thousand channels.
Meditating on the Self and restricting his diet, for as long as twelve years,
the yogi shall attain perfection through constant practice of the Siddhāsana.

What is the use of many other seats when the Siddhāsana has been mastered? When the vital breath (prāṇānila) is held with attention in the absolute kumbhaka, the state of Unmanī arises spontaneously and without effort. (HYP 1.43)
Likewise, when that one firm Siddhāsana is accomplished,
the threefold bandha arises spontaneously and without effort.
There is no posture equal to the Siddhasana; no Kumbhaka comparable to the Kevala;
no Mudrā equal to the Khecarī; and no dissolution (laya) like that of the Nāda. (HYP 1.45)
Now, regarding the lotus posture (padmāsana):
having placed the right foot upon the left thigh and likewise the left foot upon the right thigh, one should hold them firmly with both hands according to the prescribed method.
Placing the two thumbs upon the heart, one should gaze at the tip of the nose;
this is called the lotus posture (padmāsana) for self-restrained practitioners, which brings about the destruction of disease.
Having carefully placed the two feet flat and resting upon the thighs,
and likewise having placed the two hands with palms upward between the thighs, one should then fix the gaze.
One should place the tongue at the root of the upper teeth at the tip of the nose;
pressing the chin against the chest, one should slowly raise the breath.
This is declared to be the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), which destroys all diseases;
it is difficult for anyone to attain, yet it is found on earth by the wise.
Having joined the hands in the *sampuṭita* gesture, firmly assuming the *padmāsana*, and placing the chin tightly against the chest, one should meditate upon that [object] in the mind,
repeatedly exhaling the downward-moving breath (*apāna*) and filling [the abdomen] with the upward-moving air (*prāṇa*).
By the power of the Śakti, a person attains incomparable awakening as the vital breath moves downward.
The yogi seated in the lotus posture who holds the breath filled through the gateway of the *nāḍīs* is liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Now, regarding the lion posture (*siṃhāsana*): one should place the two ankles below the scrotum on either side of the perineal seam;
specifically, the left ankle on the right side and the right ankle on the left. (HYP 1.52)
Having placed both hands upon the knees and fully extended the fingers,
one should gaze at the tip of the nose with the mouth slightly open, being well-composed.
This shall be the lion-throne, honored by the foremost of yogis;
it effects the union of the three bonds and is the supreme posture.
Now, regarding the Bhadrasana:
the two heels are placed below the scrotum on both sides of the perineum;
the left heel is likewise placed on the left [side], and the right heel on the right. (HYP 1.55)
Firmly binding the sides and feet with the hands so that they are perfectly still, this shall be the Bhadrasana posture, which destroys all diseases;
indeed, the accomplished yogis call this Gorakṣāsana. (HYP 1.56)

Thus, having become free from fatigue through the various postures of sitting, the lord of yogis should practice the purification of the channels and the techniques for controlling the vital breath, such as the *mudrās*.

Posture, various breath-retentions (kumbhaka), the practice known as mudrā, and likewise the method [of practice], as well as the investigation of sound (nāda) and the sequence of training— these constitute Haṭha.
A celibate practitioner who eats moderately, practices renunciation, and is devoted to yoga shall become perfected after one year; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Food that is very smooth and sweet, consumed with one-fourth portion removed for the sake of pleasing Śiva, is called "moderate diet" (mitāhāra). HYP 1.60.
Bitter, sour, pungent, salty, and hot [foods], potherbs,
fermented grain-water (*sauvīra*), oil, sesame, mustard, liquor, fish,
the meat of goats and other animals, curd, buttermilk, horse-gram (*kulattha*), and jujube (*kola*).
They say that oil-cake, asafoetida, garlic, and similar substances are unwholesome.

One should know that food which is unwholesome, not made warm, or parched; as well as that which is excessively salty, acidic, or consists of stale, putrid, or spoiled food—these must be avoided. (HYP 1.62)
One should practice the avoidance of fire, women, and travel on roads at the beginning [of the practice].
For thus says Gorakṣa:

"One should avoid the company of the wicked, as well as fire, women, and travel on roads; likewise, one should avoid the practice of bodily mortification, such as morning baths, fasting, and the like. (HYP 1.64)
Wheat, rice, barley, ṣāṣṭika rice, and other excellent grains;
milk, ghee, sugar-candy, fresh butter, prepared sweets, and honey;
and the five vegetables beginning with ginger, pointed gourd, and kaphala.
And water from divine sources such as the Mudga spring, which flows along the path of Yama and Indra.
A yogi should partake of food that is nourishing, very sweet, unctuous, derived from cow products, which promotes the bodily constituents, is desired by the mind, and is wholesome. (HYP 1.66)
Whether young, old, very aged, diseased, or even weak, one who is untiring attains perfection through practice in all yogas. (HYP 1.67)
Success belongs to one who is engaged in practice; how could it belong to one who does not act?
The perfection of yoga is not produced by the mere recitation of the scriptures. (HYP 1.68)
Neither the wearing of [ascetic] dress nor talk thereof is the cause of perfection;
action alone is the cause of perfection—this is the truth, there is no doubt. (HYP 1.69)
The seats, the various and divine potations,
and all the methods of practice in Haṭha Yoga culminate in the fruit of Rāja Yoga.
Thus ends the first instruction in the Haṭhapradīpikā. (2) The second instruction:
Now, when the posture is firm, the yogi who has mastery over his senses and eats wholesome, moderate food...
One should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) according to the path taught by the guru.
When the breath moves, the mind moves; when it is still, the mind becomes still.
The yogi attains the state of a pillar; therefore, he should restrain the vital air.
As long as the vital air remains in the body, so long is it said to be living;
death is its departure from there, therefore one should restrain the vital air.
When the vital breath does not move through the central channel among the impure channels, how can the state of *unmanī* arise, and how can the perfection of the goal be attained? (HYP 2.4)
When the entire network of channels, which was previously clouded by impurities, becomes completely pure,
at that very moment the yogi is born capable of mastering the vital breath.

Thereafter, one should daily perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with a mind characterized by purity (*sāttvika*), so that the impurities residing within the *suṣumṇā* channel are brought to purification. (HYP 2.6)
The yogin, having assumed the bound lotus posture (baddha-padmāsana), should fill the vital breath (prāṇa) with the moon;
having retained it according to his capacity, he should exhale it again through the sun.
Having drawn in the breath through the sun (the right nostril), one should slowly fill the abdomen;
having performed the retention (kumbhaka) according to the rule, one should exhale again through the moon (the left nostril).
Having drunk with the [pipe] by which one should expel, one should retain it without obstruction;
then one should exhale through the other [nostril], very slowly indeed, and not with force.
If one should drink the breath through the *iḍā* while it is restrained, one should subsequently exhale it in the opposite manner;
having drunk the air through the *piṅgalā*, one should then bind it and release it through the *vāmā*.
By those who always perform the practice of the sun and the moon according to this method—
The groups of channels of those who practice self-restraint become purified after three months.
One should practice the *kumbhaka* breath-retentions four times a day— at dawn, midday, evening, and midnight— gradually increasing until they reach eighty in number.
In the lowest stage there is perspiration; in the middle stage there is trembling;
in the highest stage one attains stability; thereafter, one should bind the vital air.
One should perform a massage of the limbs with water produced through physical exertion;
by this, firmness and lightness of the body are produced. (HYP 2.13)
At the time of the initial practice, a diet of milk and ghee is recommended;
once the practice has become firm, such a restriction need not be observed.
Just as a lion, an elephant, or a tiger may be gradually brought under control, so too is the breath when practiced correctly; otherwise, it destroys the practitioner. (HYP 2.15)
Through properly applied breath control (prāṇāyāma), there shall be the destruction of all diseases;
through improperly practiced yoga, there arises the emergence of all diseases. (HYP 2.16)
Hiccups, labored breathing, coughing, and pains in the head, ears, and eyes—
various diseases such as these arise from the provocation of the wind (vāta).
One should exhale the breath properly and properly, and one should fill it with air properly and properly;
one should likewise restrain it properly and properly—thus one shall attain perfection.
But when the purification of the channels has occurred, then external signs certainly arise in the body: leanness and radiance. (HYP 2.19)
From the purification of the channels, the retention of breath at will, the kindling of the internal fire, the manifestation of the inner sound (nāda), and freedom from disease arise. (HYP 2.20)
One who has an excess of fat and phlegm should first perform the six purificatory acts; others, however, should not perform them because their humors are in equilibrium. (HYP 2.21)
Dhauti, Basti, Neti, Trāṭaka, Naulika, and Kapālabhāti— these are declared to be the six cleansing practices (ṣaṭkarma).
This sixfold practice, which purifies the body and brings about a variety of virtues, is kept secret and is honored by the foremost of yogis. (HYP 2.23)
Among those, *dhauti* is as follows:
one should slowly swallow a cloth, four fingers wide and fifteen cubits long, which has been moistened according to the method taught by the Guru.
One should draw this back again; that is declared to be the practice of *dhauti*.
Cough, asthma, splenic disorders, skin diseases, and the twenty types of phlegm-related illnesses undoubtedly vanish through the power of the *dhauti* practice; of this there is no doubt. (HYP 2.25)
Now, regarding enema (basti):

Standing in water reaching the navel, with the nozzle inserted into the anus and sitting in a squatting posture (utkaṭāsana), one should perform the contraction of the base (ādhāra); that is the cleansing enema procedure (basti-karma). (HYP 2.26)
Gulma, splenic enlargement, abdominal dropsy, and all diseases arising from vāta, pitta, and kapha are destroyed through the power of the enema therapy (basti-karma).
It bestows clarity upon the senses and the internal organ,
imparts a brilliance blazing like fire,
and destroys the entire accumulation of defects.
The practice of the water enema (jala-basti) is being performed.
Now, as for *neti*:
one should insert a very smooth thread of one span (*vitasti*) length into the nasal passage and draw it out through the mouth; this is called *neti* by the perfected ones (*siddhas*). (HYP 2.29)
It purifies the skull-cavity, bestows divine vision,
and the Neti practice swiftly destroys the multitude of diseases arising above the collarbone.
Now, regarding *trāṭaka*:
One should gaze at a subtle object with a steady vision, composed in meditation, until tears begin to flow; this is what the teachers have called *trāṭaka*. (HYP 2.31)
Trāṭaka is the liberation from eye diseases and the bolt against lassitude;
it should be guarded with effort, like a casket of gold. (HYP 2.32)
Now, regarding *nauli*:
with the force of rapid whirling, one whose shoulders are bent should rotate the abdomen from left to right; this is *nauli*, which is praised by the perfected ones (*siddhas*). (HYP 2.33)

This *nauli*, the crest-jewel of *haṭha* practices, always kindles the weak digestive fire, acts as a digestive catalyst, brings about healing, and produces bliss; it dries up all diseases born of the *doṣas*. (HYP 2.34)
Now, Kapālabhāti: like a blacksmith’s bellows, with rapid inhalation and exhalation, this is known as Kapālabhāti; it dries up the disorder of phlegm (kapha). (HYP 2.35)

Once the grossness of the bodily humors, phlegm, impurities, and so forth has been removed by the sixfold action (ṣaṭkarma), one should then practice breath control (prāṇāyāma); thus it is accomplished without effort.
"By means of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) alone, all impurities are dried up";
thus, for certain teachers, no other practice is approved. (HYP 2.37)
Then, having stirred the downward-moving wind (apāna) within the throat-pipe, they vomit forth the substance located in the belly by means of the elephant-like action (gajakaraṇī).
When the channels and cakras have been brought under control through gradual practice,
it is called *gajakaraṇī* by those who know Haṭha Yoga.
Even the thirty gods, beginning with Brahmā, became intent upon the practice of breath-control out of fear of Death;
therefore, one should practice prāṇāyāma.
As long as the vital breath is bound within the body, as long as the mind is undisturbed,
and as long as the gaze is fixed between the eyebrows, so long from where can there be fear of time?
When the wheel of the channels has been purified through the proper practice of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma),
the vital air enters with ease, piercing the opening of the Suṣumṇā.
Now, when the *manonmanī* wind moves through the center, steadiness of mind arises;
that state which is the perfect stabilization of the mind is itself *manonmanī*. (HYP 2.42)
To achieve that, those who know the methods perform various types of breath-retentions (*kumbhaka*).
Through the practice of diverse *kumbhakas*, one shall attain manifold accomplishments (*siddhi*). (HYP 2.43)
Now, the varieties of *kumbhaka*:
Sūryabheda, Ujjāyī, Sītkārī, Śītalī, as well as Bhastrikā, Bhrāmarī, Mūrcchā, and Plāvinī—these are the eight types of *kumbhaka*. (HYP 2.44)
At the end of inhalation (pūraka), the lock known as Jālandhara should be performed;
at the end of retention (kumbhaka) and the beginning of exhalation (recaka), the Uḍḍiyāna lock should be performed.
By quickly contracting the lower body and constricting the throat,
and by applying a backward tension in the middle, the vital breath enters the Brahma-nāḍī.
Having raised the *āpāna* upward, the yogi should lead the *prāṇa* down from the throat;
being thus liberated from old age, he shall possess the vitality of a sixteen-year-old.
Now, regarding the piercing of the sun (sūrya-bhedanam):
Having assumed a comfortable posture, the yogi should then gradually draw in the external air through the right channel (dakṣa-nāḍī). HYP 2.48.
One should retain the breath by means of kumbhaka from the hair to the tips of the nails until cessation;
then, one should slowly exhale the air through the left channel (nāḍī).
It purifies the skull, destroys disorders of wind (vāta), and removes the affliction of worms;
this supreme Sūryabheda [prāṇāyāma] should be performed again and again.

Now, having restrained the mouth in the *ujjāyī* [breathing technique], one should slowly draw the breath through the two channels so that it resonates as it passes from the throat down to the heart. (HYP 2.51)
As before, one should retain the breath and then exhale through the *iḍā*;
this removes phlegm disorders from the throat and increases the digestive fire of the body. (HYP 2.52)
The practice known as *ujjāyī* kumbhaka should be performed while walking or standing; it destroys disorders located in the channels, the abdomen, and the bodily constituents (*dhātus*). (HYP 2.53)
Then, one should make the sound "sīt"; likewise, one should perform yawning through the mouth and the nose.
By means of such practice, one becomes a second Kāmadeva. (HYP 2.54)
Honored by the circle of Yoginīs, he is the agent of creation and dissolution;
neither hunger nor thirst, nor sleep nor even laziness arises in him.
And by this method, the lord of yogis shall truly become a being on the surface of the earth who is free from all afflictions.
Now, for *śītalī*:
having drawn in the air with the tongue as before, the wise practitioner performs the practice of *kumbhaka* and should slowly exhale the breath through both nostrils. (HYP 2.57)
Indeed, this Kumbhikā named Śītalī destroys diseases such as gulma and splenic disorders, as well as fever, bile, hunger, thirst, and poisons. (HYP 2.58)
Then, having placed both soles of the feet auspiciously upon the thighs,
this shall be the lotus posture (padmāsana), which destroys all evil.
Having correctly assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), with neck and abdomen held straight, the wise one,
having carefully restrained the mouth, should exhale the breath through the nose.
Just as it resonates from the heart and throat up to the skull,
one should also forcefully fill the vital air (māruta) up to the lotus of the heart.
One should purge again in that same manner and fill [the body] again and again,
just as a blacksmith moves a bellows with force.
In that very same way, one should mentally move the vital air situated within one's own body;
when fatigue arises in the body, then one should fill it with the solar breath.
Just as the abdomen becomes full [of air], it likewise becomes light;
one should hold the nose firmly with the middle and index fingers, excluding the thumb. (HYP 2.64)
Having performed the *kumbhaka* according to the rules, one should exhale the breath through the *iḍā*.
This removes wind, bile, and phlegm, and increases the digestive fire of the body.
Kuṇḍalī-bodhaka quickly awakens the vital wind (pavana), bestows happiness, and is beneficial;
it destroys the obstructions of phlegm and other humors situated at the opening of the Brahma-nāḍī.
This kumbhaka known as *bhastrā* must be performed specifically in order to pierce the three knots that have arisen within the body. (HYP 2.67)

Then, through the force of *bhrāmarī*, [one performs] inhalation (*pūraka*) with a humming sound like the buzzing of a bee (*bhṛṅga-nāda*) or the song of a female bee (*bhṛṅgī-nāda*), and exhalation (*recaka*) very slowly.
Thus, through the yoga of practice, a certain play of bliss arises in the mind of the Queen of Yogis.

Then, at the end of the *pūraka*, having bound the *jālandhara* lock very firmly, one should slowly exhale; this is called *mūrchā*, which brings about the bliss of mental absorption (*manomūrchā*). (HYP 2.69)
Then, with his abdomen filled by the noble wind circulating within,
he floats easily even in fathomless water like a lotus leaf. (HYP 2.70)
Prāṇāyāma is said to be threefold by means of exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka); it is considered to be of two kinds: sahita (conjoined) and kevala (pure). HYP 2.71.
One should practice this together until complete perfection is attained;
that is, the comfortable retention of the vital breath (vāyu), having abandoned both exhalation and inhalation.
This is called breath control (*prāṇāyāma*); it is indeed the pure *kumbhaka*.
When the pure *kumbhaka*, devoid of exhalation and inhalation, has been mastered, [one attains success]. (HYP 2.73)
Nothing whatsoever in the three worlds is difficult for him to obtain,
since he is capable of retaining the breath at will by means of the single-jar [kumbhaka] alone.
One also attains the state of Rāja-yoga; of this there is no doubt.
From Kumbhaka comes the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī, and from the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī, the Suṣumṇā becomes unobstructed and the perfection of Haṭha-yoga arises.
Without Haṭha there is no Rājayoga, and without Rājayoga there is no success in Haṭha; therefore, one should practice the pair together until perfection is attained.
At the conclusion of the retention of breath (*kumbhaka*), one should make the mind supportless;
through such practice of yoga, one shall attain the state of *rājayoga*.
Emaciation of the body, clarity in the face, distinctness in the sound, the eyes being perfectly clear,
freedom from disease, mastery over the *bindu*, and stimulation of the digestive fire.
The purification of the channels is the characteristic sign of success in Haṭha-yoga.
Thus ends the second instruction in the Haṭhapradīpikā.
The third instruction:
Just as the serpent-king is the support for the mountains, forests, and the earth;
For Kuṇḍalinī is indeed the support of all Yoga-tantras.
When Kuṇḍalinī, sleeping by the grace of the Guru, awakens,
then all the lotuses and even the knots are pierced.
Then the path of the void becomes like a royal highway for the vital breath;
then the mind is without support, and then there is the deception of time.
Suṣumṇā, Śūnyapadavī, Brahmarandhra, Mahāpatha, Śmaśāna, Śāmbhavī, and Madhyamārga—these are synonyms. (HYP 3.4)
Therefore, with every effort, one should practice the application of the mudrās upon the gateway of Brahmā, where the Goddess sleeps, in order to awaken her. (HYP 3.5)
Mahāmudrā, the great seal; the great bond (mahābandha); the great penetration (mahāvedha); Khecarī; Uḍḍīyāna; Mūlabandha; and the bond known as Jālandhara. (HYP 3.6)
Karaṇī, the one called Viparītā, Vajrolī, and Śakticālana—this indeed is the tenfold set of mudrās that destroys old age and death. (HYP 3.7)
This divine [teaching] was proclaimed by the Primordial Lord; it bestows the eight sovereign powers, is beloved by all the Siddhas, and is difficult even for the gods to attain.
It should be guarded with great effort, like a casket of jewels; it must never be told to anyone, just as the secret amorous dalliance of a woman of noble family is kept hidden.
Then, having pressed the vulva with the left foot at its base and extending the right foot,
one should hold [the body] firmly with both hands. (HYP 3.10)
Having applied the binding at the throat, one should hold the breath upwards;
just as a snake struck by a staff becomes straight like a staff.
When the śakti, which is coiled like a serpent, suddenly becomes straightened,
then that state of death arises, resting upon the two petals.
Then one should exhale very slowly indeed, and not with force;
by that very method, the supreme wise ones call it Mahāmudrā.
This very Mahāmudrā has been revealed by the great adepts;
the defects such as the great afflictions and death and so forth are exhausted.
Therefore, the best of the wise call it Mahāmudrā.
Having practiced thoroughly on the lunar limb, one should practice again on the solar limb until the count becomes equal; then, one should release the mudrā.
For indeed, whether wholesome or unwholesome, all tastes are not devoid of flavor;
even dreadful poison, once consumed, is digested, and even nectar likewise passes away.
Consumption, leprosy, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, indigestion, and other such ailments—his humors go to destruction if he practices Mahāmudrā. (HYP 3.17)
This Mahāmudrā, which brings about great accomplishment for human beings, has been taught; it should be guarded with effort and not given to just anyone. HYP 3.18.
Now, the Mahābandha:
One should place the heel of the left foot in the region of the perineum, and likewise place the right foot upon the left thigh. (HYP 3.19)
Then, having filled the breath, one should firmly press the chin against the heart;
contracting the breath, one should force it into the center of the mind.
Having retained [the breath] according to one's capacity, one should slowly exhale the air;
having practiced on the left side, one should then practice on the right side.
In this regard, however, some hold the view that one should avoid binding the throat;
rather, the binding of the tongue against the upper teeth is said to be recommended. (HYP 3.22)
But this [bandha] is the obstructor of the upward movement of all the channels;
indeed, it is the Great Bandha that bestows great accomplishment.
Expert in liberating one from the great bondage of the noose of Time, he maintains the confluence of the three rivers; let him lead the mind to Kedāra.

Just as a woman endowed with beauty and charm is [useless] without a man, so too the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) and the Great Bond (mahābandha) are fruitless when devoid of penetration (vedha). (HYP 3.25)
Now, regarding the Great Piercing (mahā-vedha):

the yogi, established in the Great Lock (mahā-bandha), single-mindedly performs inhalation (pūraka) and, by means of the throat-seal (kaṇṭha-mudrā), quietly obstructs the movement of the vital airs. (HYP 3.26)
With the two hands placed evenly on the ground, one should slowly press down upon the buttocks;
having passed beyond the two nostrils, the wind throbs as it moves through the center.
Indeed, a connection between Soma, Sūrya, and Agni arises for the sake of immortality;
when the state of death has arisen, one should then exhale the breath through Vāyu.
This Great Piercing, through practice, bestows great accomplishment;
it destroys wrinkles, graying hair, and trembling, and is cultivated by the most excellent practitioners. (HYP 3.29)
This triad is a great secret that destroys old age and death;
it increases the digestive fire and bestows the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
It is performed eight times, every watch and day after day,
for the sake of accumulating merit and for the constant destruction of the flood of evil.
For those who possess the right training, this is the first practice, though it is very brief.
Now, when the tongue enters the hollow of the skull and moves in reverse,
and the gaze is fixed between the eyebrows, that is the Khecarī Mudrā. (HYP 3.32)
Then, by means of cutting, shaking, and milking, one should gradually increase the *kalā* until it touches the space between the eyebrows; at that time, the perfection of Khecarī is attained.
Then, taking up a weapon resembling the leaf of the *snuhī* plant— extremely sharp, smooth, and stainless— one should cut away only a single hair with it.
Then, one should rub [the area] with powdered saindhava and pathyā;
when seven days have passed again, one should shave it down to the level of the hair.
In this manner, one who is constantly disciplined should practice for six months in succession;
after six months, the binding of the vessels at the root of the tongue is destroyed.
Having turned the *kalā* away from the face and joined it at the *tripatha*, that becomes the *khecarī-mudrā*; it is called the *vyomacakra*.
If the yogi holds the tongue upward for even half a moment,
he is liberated from poisons, as well as from disease, death, old age, and the like.
Neither disease, nor death, nor lassitude, nor sleep, nor hunger, nor thirst,
nor even fainting shall befall him who knows the Khecarī Mudrā.
He who knows the Khecarī Mudrā is not afflicted by disease, is not tainted by karma, and is not oppressed by time.
Because the mind moves in the void and the tongue has gone to move in the void,
this mudrā is designated by the Siddhas as Khecarī.
He by whom the aperture above the uvula is sealed by means of the Khecarī [mudrā],
his bindu does not leak, even when he is embraced by a passionate woman.
Even when the drop has moved and reached the circle of the womb,
it goes upward, drawn back by the Śakti and bound by the Yoni-mudrā.
The knower of yoga who, having become steady, performs the drinking of soma with his tongue turned upward,
undoubtedly conquers death within half a month.
The poison does not spread within that yogi whose body is eternally filled with the digits of the moon, even if he has been bitten by Takṣaka.
Just as fire does not leave its fuel, nor a lamp its oil and wick,
so the embodied soul, filled with the digits of the moon, does not abandon the body.
One who constantly eats beef and drinks the nectar of immortality (amaravāruṇī)—him I consider noble; others are destroyers of their lineage.
The tongue is denoted by the word "go" (cow);
its entry into the palate is indeed the consumption of cow-flesh, which destroys even the greatest sins.
Indeed, that essence which flows from the moon, produced by the fire generated through the entry of the tongue, is the nectar of the immortals.
If the tongue, dripping with saliva, constantly kisses the tip of the uvula—
whether that saliva be alkaline, pungent, sour, or like milk, or likewise like honey and clarified butter—
it effects the removal of diseases, brings an end to old age, and wards off the onset of weapons.
For him there shall be immortality eightfold, as well as the power of attracting the women of the Siddhas.

He who, with his face turned upward, having forcefully restrained the tongue in the cavity [of the uvula] and focused his mind on the supreme power (śakti), drinks the pure stream consisting of waves of nectar that has flowed from the sixteen-petaled lotus at the crown and been obtained from the vital breath (prāṇa).
Free from disease, with a body as delicate as a lotus stalk, that yogi lives for a long time.
The wise one declares that the reality [of death] resides in that frost which, having been sent forth through the hollows, stays within the summit of Meru;
from the moon, the essence flows from its body, and by that, the death of men occurs.
One should bind that in a comfortable manner below; otherwise, there is no perfection of the body.
The hollow space that generates knowledge and is endowed with five channels—
therein, within that void and stainless state, the Khecarī Mudrā abides.
There is one seed-syllable consisting of creation, and one mudrā, which is khecarī;
there is one god who is without support, and one state, which is manonmanī.
Now, the Uḍḍīyāna-bandha:
Because by means of this [bandha] the vital breath (prāṇa) is bound within the Suṣumṇā and ascends upward, it is therefore proclaimed by yogis as "Uḍḍīyāna" (the Flying). (HYP 3.55)
Because the great bird flies upward without ceasing, that very act is called Uḍḍīyāna; it is described as your [the yogi's] bond.
One should perform the posterior contraction of the abdomen above the navel;
for this is the Uḍḍīyāna Bandha, the lion that destroys the elephant of death.
Uḍḍīyāna is indeed innate, as taught by the Guru at all times;
he who practices it constantly becomes youthful even if he is old.
One should diligently perform the expansion [of the breath] both above and below the navel;
by practicing this for six months, one certainly conquers death—of this there is no doubt.
Of all the locks indeed, Uḍḍīyānaka is the highest;
when the lock of Uḍḍīyāna is firmly established, liberation becomes natural.
Now, the Mūlabandha:
pressing the perineum with the heel and contracting the anus, one draws the apāna upward; this is called Mūlabandha. (HYP 3.61)
By means of contraction, one forcibly causes the downward-moving *apāna* to go upward;
indeed, yogis call this the *mūla-bandha*.
Pressing the anus with the heel,
one should forcefully contract the wind so that the vital air repeatedly moves upward.
When the prāṇa and apāna, as well as nāda and bindu, attain oneness through the mūlabandha, they bestow the perfect accomplishment of yoga; of this there is no doubt.
The unification of the apāna and prāṇa breaths and the cessation of urine and feces occur through the constant practice of mūlabandha; even an old man becomes young again.
When the apāna rises upward and enters the circle of fire,
then a long flame of fire arises, struck by the wind.
Then, having gone from there, it reaches the fire and the downward breath (apāna), as well as the upward breath (prāṇa) whose nature is heat;
by that [heat], the fire born of the body becomes intensely inflamed.
By that [means], the sleeping Kuṇḍalinī, being heated, becomes fully awakened;
like a female serpent struck by a staff, she hisses and attains straightness.
Then, as if entering a well, one should proceed through the channel of Brahmā;
therefore, yogis should always constantly perform the root-lock (mūla-bandha).
Now, the Jālandhara Bandha: Contracting the throat, one should firmly place the chin against the heart;
this is the bandha called Jālandhara, which destroys old age and death. (HYP 3.70)
For it binds the network of vessels that carry the water of the sky downward;
therefore, Jālandhara-bandha is the destroyer of the flood of suffering in the throat. (HYP 3.71)
When the Jālandhara lock is performed, characterized by the contraction of the throat, the nectar does not fall into the fire, nor does the vital wind become disturbed. (HYP 3.72)
By means of constricting the throat alone, one should firmly restrain the two channels;
this is to be known as the middle wheel, the binding of the sixteen supports.
Having firmly contracted the root-center (mūla-sthāna), one should perform the uḍḍīyāna lock;
having bound both the iḍā and piṅgalā, one should cause [the breath] to flow along the western path.
By this very method, the vital breath (pavana) goes to dissolution;
consequently, neither birth nor death, nor likewise old age, disease, and so forth, arise.
These three bindings are the most excellent, practiced by the great Siddhas;
yogis know them to be the means for accomplishing all Haṭha Tantras. (HYP 3.76)
Whatever nectar flows from the moon, which possesses a divine form, the sun swallows it all; by that, the physical body becomes subject to decay.
Now follows the *viparītakaraṇī* mudrā; therein lies a divine method for deceiving the mouth of the sun.
It is to be known through the instruction of the Guru, and not by means of millions of scriptural interpretations. (HYP 3.78)
Above the navel and below the palate is the sun above and the moon below;
this inverted posture (viparītākaraṇī) is obtained through the word of the Guru.
For the practitioner who is constantly engaged in practice, abundant food that increases the digestive fire should be provided.
If the fire [of digestion] becomes weak due to meager food, it burns [the body] instantly;
therefore, on the first day, one should remain for a moment with the head downward and the feet upward.
And if one practices for even slightly more than a moment day after day,
wrinkles and gray hair will no longer be seen after six months;
however, he who practices constantly for the duration of a single watch (yāma) is a conqueror of time.
Now, even if one acts according to one's own will without the restraints prescribed for yoga,
he who understands *vajrolī* is a yogi who becomes a vessel for accomplishment. (HYP 3.83)
In this regard, I shall describe two things that are difficult for anyone to obtain:
first, milk; and second, a woman who is submissive. (HYP 3.84)
By practicing the upward contraction properly and gradually with effort,
both man and woman shall attain the perfection of Vajrolī.
One should slowly and gently perform blowing through the praised stalk into the vajra-cavity, with effort, for the sake of setting the vital winds in motion.
By practice, one should draw upward the drop from the female organ;
and having drawn upward one's own drop when it has moved, one should preserve it.
Thus, by guarding the *bindu*, the knower of yoga triumphs;
death occurs through the falling of the *bindu*, and life through the retention of the *bindu*.
A sweet fragrance arises in the body of the yogi from the retention of the *bindu*;
as long as the *bindu* remains stable in the body, whence can there be fear of time? (HYP 3.89)
The semen of men is dependent on the mind, and life is dependent on the semen;
therefore, one must protect both the semen and the mind with great effort.
Likewise, a woman in her menses should protect her own discharge;
one who knows the yoga of proper practice should draw it upward by means of the penis.
Now, the Sahajoli:
The Sahajoli and the Cāmaroli are both variations of the Vajrolī;
having cast pure ash produced from burnt cow dung into water. (HYP 3.92)

From the practice of Vajrolī during sexual union, the fluids of both the woman and the man are smeared upon their own bodies; this occurs spontaneously and effortlessly in an instant for those who remain seated and free from exertion.
This is declared to be Sahajoli, which should always be practiced with faith by yogis;
this auspicious yoga bestows liberation even while one is engaged in worldly enjoyment.
This yoga succeeds for those who possess merit, who are steadfast, who perceive reality, and who are free from envy; it does not succeed for those characterized by envy.
Now, regarding Amarolī:
because of the predominance of bile, one should avoid the first stream of water and take the final stream due to its lack of essence.
The cool, middle stream is practiced by the Kāpālikas; in the Khaṇḍamata, it is called Amarolī.
He who daily drinks the *amarī* and applies it as a nasal drop day after day, and practices the *vajrolī* correctly, is said to be a *sāmarolī*. (HYP 3.97)
One should mix the lunar nectar, which has emerged through practice, with the [elemental] powers;
by holding it upon the crown of the head, divine vision is produced.
If a woman, by properly contracting her *bindu* through proficiency in practice,
can preserve her menstrual flow (*rajas*) by means of *vajrolī*, she too is a *yoginī*.
Not even a trace of her menstrual flow perishes, of this there is no doubt;
within her body, the *nāda* indeed attains the state of the *bindu*.
That *bindu* and that *rajas*, having become unified within one's own body through the practice of *vajrolī*, bestow all spiritual accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*).
One should guard [the breath] above its contraction; for that *rajas* is indeed the Yoginī.
She knows the past and the future, and one certainly becomes a Khecarī.
And one attains the perfection of the body through the practice of *vajrolī*.
This meritorious yoga bestows liberation even while enjoying worldly pleasures. (HYP 3.103)
Now, the movement of the *śakti*:
"The crooked-bodied one, Kuṇḍalinī, Bhujaṅgī, Śakti, Īśvarī, Kuṇḍalī, and Arundhatī—these are synonymous terms. (HYP 3.104)
Just as one might forcibly open a door with a key,
so too should the yogi pierce the gate of liberation by means of Kuṇḍalinī.
The Supreme Goddess, having covered with her mouth that path by which one must go to the stainless abode of Brahmā, lies fast asleep.
Above the *kanda* lies the Kuṇḍalinī energy, which is dormant; she leads to liberation for yogins, but to bondage for the deluded—he who knows her is a knower of Yoga. (HYP 3.107)
Kuṇḍalinī is proclaimed to be coiled in shape like a serpent;
he by whom that power is set in motion is liberated—of this there is no doubt.
Between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, one who should forcibly seize an ascetic widow— that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
The goddess Iḍā is the Gaṅgā river, and Piṅgalā is the Yamunā river;
between Iḍā and Piṅgalā are Bālaraṇḍā and Kuṇḍalī.
Grasping the serpent by its tail, one should awaken it while it is asleep;
having abandoned sleep, that power rises up forcefully.
Remaining there as a serpent,
she would, at both morning and evening for half a watch,
completely fill [the space] from the sun by means of her expanded hood.
Having grasped it, one should constantly move it back and forth.
One span in height and four finger-breadths in width,
soft and white— this is described as the characteristic of the cloth for wrapping.
When seated in the vajra posture, one should firmly hold the feet with both hands near the region of the ankles and press upon the *kanda* there.
Seated in the vajra posture, the yogi, having moved the kuṇḍalī, should immediately perform the bellows-breathing (bhastrā); this will quickly awaken the kuṇḍalī. (HYP 3.115)
One should perform the contraction of the sun (the solar channel) and then move Kuṇḍalinī;
for such a person, even if they have entered the mouth of Death, whence can there be fear of death? (HYP 3.116)
By moving it fearlessly for a period of two muhūrtas,
it is drawn slightly upward and rises within the suṣumṇā.
Because of that, Kuṇḍalinī certainly leaves the mouth of that Suṣumṇā;
therefore, this vital breath (prāṇa) enters the Suṣumṇā of its own accord.
Therefore, one should constantly move Arundhatī while she is sleeping happily;
by moving her alone, the yogi is liberated from diseases. (HYP 3.119)
The yogin by whom the power (śakti) has been set in motion is a vessel for accomplishment;
what is the use of much speaking on this matter? He conquers time with ease.
Success is seen from the maṇḍala for one who delights in celibacy, who always eats wholesome and moderate food, and who is a yogin practicing the discipline of Kuṇḍalinī.
Having set the Kuṇḍalinī in motion, one should especially practice the bellows-breathing (bhastrā).
For the self-controlled practitioner who thus practices constantly, whence can there be fear of death? (HYP 3.122)
Regarding the purification of the impurities of the seventy-two thousand channels, what means of washing exists other than the practice of Kuṇḍalinī? (HYP 3.123)
However, this central channel (madhyamā-nāḍī) becomes straight for yogins through firm practice, by means of postures (āsana), control of the vital breath (prāṇa-saṃyāma), and mudrās. (HYP 3.124)
But for those who are sleepless in their practice, having fixed the mind through meditative absorption (samādhi),
either Rudrāṇī or the supreme Mudrā bestows auspicious perfection (siddhi).
Without Rāja-yoga, the earth [is not truly the earth]; without Rāja-yoga, the night [is not truly the night];
without Rāja-yoga, even a manifold mudrā does not shine.
One should practice the entire procedure for the vital air (māruta) with a concentrated mind;
the wise person should not allow the activity of the mind to wander elsewhere. (HYP 3.127)
Thus have the ten mudrās been proclaimed by Śambhu, the Primordial Lord;
among them, each one bestows great siddhi upon those who practice self-restraint.
He who imparts the traditional instruction on the mudrās is indeed the venerable Guru, the Master; he is the Lord himself in visible form. (HYP 3.129)
Becoming intent upon his word and concentrated in the practice of mudrā,
one attains the deception of time along with the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā).
Thus ends the third instruction in the Haṭhapradīpikā. (4) The fourth instruction:
Salutations to the Guru Śiva, whose nature consists of Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā.
One who has that as his ultimate goal constantly attains the stainless state.
Now, therefore, I shall proclaim the supreme sequence of meditative absorption (samādhi),
which destroys death, is an easy means [to liberation], and brings about the highest bliss of Brahman.
Rāja-yoga, samādhi, unmanī, and manonmanī;
immortality, dissolution, the ultimate reality, the void and the non-void—the supreme state.
The mindless, the non-dual, the supportless, the stainless,
liberation while living, the innate, and the fourth state— these are synonyms for one and the same reality.
Just as rock salt attains a state of equilibrium when joined with water,
so too the unification of the self and the mind is designated as *samādhi*.
When the vital breath is completely attenuated and the mind dissolves,
that state of equal flavor is designated as *samādhi*.
And the oneness of those two—the individual self and the supreme self—is equal to that;
when all mental constructs have perished, that is designated as samādhi.
Who truly knows the greatness of Rāja-yoga?
Knowledge, liberation, steadfastness, and perfection are obtained through the word of the Guru.
Renunciation of sense objects is difficult to attain; the vision of reality is difficult to attain;
and the innate state is difficult to attain without the compassion of a true guru. (HYP 4.9)
By means of various postures, crooked positions, and diverse techniques,
when the Great Power is awakened, the vital breath dissolves into the void.
For the yogin who has awakened the latent power and abandoned all karma without exception,
the state of the innate arises spontaneously.
When the vital breath flowing through the *suṣumṇā* enters the void within the mind, then the knower of yoga eradicates all karmas from their very root. (HYP 4.12)
Homage to you, O Immortal; even Time itself has been conquered by you—he into whose mouth this entire world of moving and unmoving beings has fallen.
When the mind has attained equanimity and the vital breath moves into the central channel,
then Amaroli, Vajroli, and Sahajoli arise.
How can knowledge arise in the mind here, as long as the vital breath lives while the mind does not die?
He who brings both this vital breath and the mind to dissolution—
That man attains liberation; no other does so in any way whatsoever.
Having understood the true division of the *suṣumṇā* and having brought the vital air (*vāyu*) into the middle path,
one should remain always in the excellent place and restrain [the breath] within the aperture of Brahmā (*brahma-randhra*).
The sun and the moon sustain time, which consists of night and day;
Suṣumnā is the consumer of that time—this is declared to be the secret.
There are seventy-two thousand channel-gates in the cage;
Suṣumṇā is the Śāmbhavī power, while the others are indeed useless.
Because the vital air (vāyu) is well-acquainted with the fire,
it awakens the Kuṇḍalinī and enters the Suṣumṇā without obstruction.
When the vital breath flows through the *suṣumṇā*, the state of *manonmanī* is indeed accomplished;
otherwise, the practices of other [channels] result only in exhaustion for yogins. (HYP 4.20)
By that which the breath is bound, by that very thing the mind is bound;
and by that which the mind is bound, by that the breath is bound. (HYP 4.21)
The two causes of the mind are its latent impressions and the vital breath;
when one of these two is destroyed, both are destroyed.
Where the mind dissolves, there the vital breath dissolves;
where the vital breath dissolves, there the mind dissolves. (HYP 4.23)
For those two, the mind and the vital breath, are joined like milk and water and perform identical functions;
since the breath exists there, so too does the activity of the mind.
For where the mind is, there the movement of the vital breath occurs.
In that regard, from the destruction of one comes the destruction of the other;
from the activity of one comes the activity of the other;
and their temporal states consist in the functioning of the group of sense faculties.
Through the destruction of these two, the accomplishment of the state of liberation is attained.
The fickleness of both the senses and the mind is inherent by nature;
when the senses are bound and the mind is bound, what on this earth cannot be accomplished?
O Pārvatī, when swooned, the mercury removes diseases; when dead, it revives by itself;
and when bound, it bestows the power of moving through the sky—so too does the vital air (vāyu).
When the mind is steady, the vital breath becomes steady; from that, the *bindu* becomes steady.
Through the steadiness of the *bindu*, the essence (*sattva*) is always present, and the steadiness of the physical body (*piṇḍa*) arises.
The mind is the lord of the senses; the vital breath (māruta) is the lord of the mind. The dissolution of the vital breath is its lord, and that dissolution rests upon sound (nāda).
Let this very state be what is called liberation, or let it not be according to other systems;
nevertheless, a certain bliss arises when the mind and vital breath are dissolved.

Victorious is the dissolution (*laya*) of the yogis, in which inhalation and exhalation have perished, the perception of sense objects has been destroyed, and one is motionless and free from transformation. (HYP 4.31)
With all conceptual constructions severed and all activities entirely exhausted,
there arises a certain dissolution that is beyond the reach of speech and can only be realized by oneself.
Wherever there is vision, there is the dissolution of the elements and the senses;
that is the power of living beings when both have dissolved into the unperceivable.
"They speak of 'laya,' 'laya'—what is the characteristic of *laya*?
*Laya* is the forgetting of sense objects due to the non-arising of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) again. (HYP 4.34)
The Vedas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas are like common courtesans;
the single Mudrā of Śambhu alone is like a secret, noble wife.
Now, the Śāmbhavī [mudrā]:
the focal point is within, while the gaze is directed outward, free from blinking or opening the eyes;
this is that Śāmbhavī mudrā, which is concealed in the Vedas and the Śāstras. (HYP 4.36)
When the yogi remains with his mind and breath dissolved within the inner mark (antarlakṣya),
looking outward below with a steady gaze while yet seeing nothing— even though he sees— he possesses this very Śāmbhavī Mudrā, which is indeed attained through the grace of the Guru.
That reality, which is characterized by neither emptiness nor non-emptiness, flashes forth as the state of Śambhu.
And through the distinction between the state (*avasthā*) and the abode (*dhāma*) of Śrī-Śāmbhavī and Khecarī,
there arises the bliss of the dissolution of the mind in the Void, which is the very form of the bliss of consciousness.
Having joined [the mind] with the light at the *tāra*, one should slightly raise the eyebrows;
by yoking the mind to the previous yoga, one becomes *unmanī* (transcending the mind) in an instant.
Some are bewildered by the web of sacred scriptures, some by the complexities of logic, and some by reasoning; they do not know the Star that leads across.
With eyes half-closed, mind steady, and gaze fixed on the tip of the nose,
he— by means of his motionless state— causes even the sun and moon to enter into dissolution;
[he beholds] that supreme, all-pervading seed of everything, resplendent in the form of light.
That reality attains that state; it is the supreme object, what more need be said here?
One should not worship the *liṅga* by day, nor should one worship it at night;
one should always worship the *liṅga* by transcending both day and night.
Now, when the vital breath, which resides in the left and right channels, moves into the middle,
the Khecarī Mudrā remains in that state; of this there is no doubt.
One should swallow the void and the vital air between the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*;
there the *khecarī* mudrā abides—this is the truth again and again.
Furthermore, that which is situated within the wheel of space, in the supportless interval between the sun and the moon, is called the *mudrā* known as Khecarī.
Where the stream arises from the *soma*, that [stream] is the manifest beloved of Śiva;
it fills the incomparable, divine *suṣumṇā* at its western opening.
When it is filled from the front, Khecarī becomes certain;
once Khecarī Mudrā has been practiced, the state of Unmanī arises.
Between the eyebrows is the abode of Śiva; there the mind dissolves. That state should be known as the Fourth (turya); therein time does not exist.
One should practice Khecarī until one is asleep in Yoga;
for one who has attained the sleep of Yoga, there is never any [limited] time.
Having made the mind supportless, one should not think of anything at all;
like a pot in space, it remains firmly established within and without.
Just as the external wind subsides, so too does the internal one; without doubt, the vital breath attains stability in its own place together with the mind.
For one who practices thus day and night upon the path of the vital breath,
the breath is digested through practice, and the mind dissolves right there.
One should flood the body with nectars from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head;
thus one indeed becomes perfected as a great-bodied being of immense strength and prowess.
Having placed the mind within the *śakti*, and the *śakti* within the middle of the mind,
one should perceive the mind with the mind and hold fast to the supreme state.
Place yourself in the midst of space, and place space in the midst of yourself;
having made everything consist of space, one should not think of anything at all.
Empty within and empty without, like an empty jar in the sky;
full within and full without, like a full jar in the ocean.
One should not engage in external thought, nor likewise internal reflection;
having abandoned all thought, one should not think of anything at all.
The entire universe is merely a construction of volition;
it is merely a construction of volition, the play of the mind.
Abandon the notion that it is merely volition, and become free from conceptualization.
Relying upon this certainty, O Rāma, attain peace.
Just as camphor dissolves in fire and rock salt in water,
so too the mind, when properly integrated, dissolves into the Reality.
All that is to be known is realized, and knowledge is called the mind;
when knowledge and the object of knowledge have equally vanished, there is no other second path.
All this that is visible to the mind—whatever exists, whether moving or unmoving—is indeed [the mind];
for when the mind becomes transcendent (unmanī-bhāva), duality is no longer perceived at all.
Through the relinquishing of the objects of knowledge, the mind dissolves;
when the dissolution of the mind has occurred, absolute liberation remains.
Thus, various types of skillful means, accompanied by one's own authentic experience,
have been described as paths to meditative absorption by the great-souled former teachers.
Salutations to you, O Suṣumṇā, Kuṇḍalinī, Sudhā, born of the Moon, Manonmanī—the Great Power whose self is consciousness. HYP 4.64.
The worship of Nāda, which has been proclaimed by the Lord Gorakṣanātha, is said to be approved even by the ignorant who are unable to realize the true reality. HYP 4.65.

The glorious Ādinātha has proclaimed that there are ten million modes of absorption (laya); may [this teaching] be victorious! Yet, there is only one [mode], which is the contemplation of the resonance (nādānusandhāna).
We consider this to be the foremost among all forms of dissolution.
Seated in the liberated posture (muktāsana), the yogi, maintaining the Śāmbhavī mudrā with one-pointed mind, should listen to the internal sound within the right ear.
The blocking of the two ears, the two eyes, the nostrils, and the mouth should be performed within the pure channel of the Suṣumṇā.
A clear and stainless sound is heard.
In all yogic practices, there are four stages: the initial undertaking, the pot-like stage, as well as the stage of familiarity, and finally, perfection. (HYP 4.69)
Now, regarding the stage of commencement:
indeed, when the knot of Brahman is pierced, there arises bliss born of the void;
a diverse resonance, the unstruck sound (*anāhata*), is heard within the body. (HYP 4.70)
Possessing a divine body, radiant, with a divine fragrance and free from disease,
one whose heart is fulfilled yet remains empty at the outset shall become a master of yoga.
Then, in the second stage, that of the jar (ghaṭāvasthā), having formed the jar, the wind becomes central;
the yogi then becomes firm in posture, a knower, and equal to a god. (HYP 4.72)

Then, from the bursting of the Viṣṇu-knot, there arises the "Churning" (vimarda), which indicates supreme bliss; at that time, in the state of extreme emptiness, there occurs the sound of a kettledrum.
Now, regarding the stage of familiarity:
"In the third [stage], however, the sound of a mardala drum in the sky is to be known;
then one enters the Great Void, which is the support for all accomplishments. (HYP 4.74)
Then, having conquered the bliss of the mind, there arises the innate bliss (sahajānanda),
which is free from defects, suffering, old age, disease, hunger, and sleep.
Then, when the vital breath (anila), having pierced the Rudra-knot at the stage of completion, reaches the seat of Śarva,
there arises at the time of completion a bamboo-like sound like the resonance of a vibrating lute.
Then the mind becomes unified, designated as royal yoga (rāja-yoga);
he becomes equal to a lord of yogis, a creator and destroyer of the universe.
Whether liberation occurs or not, here alone is unbroken happiness;
this bliss arising from absorption is attained through Rāja-yoga.
I consider those who, not knowing royal yoga, are merely practitioners of haṭha, to be mere exponents of practice who are devoid of the fruit of their exertion.
For the swift attainment of the *unmanī* state, meditation on the space between the eyebrows is my preferred method;
it is an easy means for those of limited intellect to reach the stage of *rāja-yoga*.
Through this, a dissolution born of *nāda* arises, which brings about immediate realization.
The singular bliss, inaccessible to words, which increases in the hearts of the lords of yogis who partake in the samādhi of following the inner sound (nāda).
The illustrious Guru-Nātha alone knows that.
Covering his ears with both hands, the sage should fix his mind upon whatever sound he hears, until he attains the state of stability.
This sound, when practiced, veils external noise;
after a fortnight, having conquered all distraction, the yogi becomes happy.
It is heard that at the first stage of practice, the sound is various and great;
then, as the practice increases, a subtler and subtler sound is heard.
In the beginning, there arise sounds produced by the ocean, clouds, kettledrums, and cymbals;
in the middle, those arising from the mṛdaṅga drum and the conch, as well as from the bell and the kāhala trumpet.
But before that, various kinds of sounds—such as the tinkling of small bells, the flute, the lute, and the humming of bees—are heard arising from within the body. (HYP 4.86)
Even when loud sounds such as those of clouds or kettledrums are heard,
one should there contemplate only the sound that is subtler than the subtle.
Whether it delights in the gross while abandoning the subtle, or in the subtle while abandoning the gross,
one should not allow the distracted mind to move elsewhere.
Wherever the mind first settles upon a sound, having become perfectly steady right there, it dissolves along with that sound.
Just as a bee drinking nectar has no regard for its fragrance,
so too the mind attached to the inner sound (nāda) does not long for sense objects.
This sound-sharp goad is capable of restraining the lordly elephant of the mind as it wanders through the pleasure gardens of the sense-objects.
But when the mind, having abandoned its fickleness, is bound by the bond of *nāda*,
it attains extreme steadiness, like a bird whose wings have been clipped.
Having abandoned all thought, one who desires the sovereignty of Yoga should, with an attentive mind, pursue the resonance alone.
Sound acts like a snare for binding the deer of the inner self,
and it also acts like a hunter for the slaughter of that inner deer.
The internal restraint of the senses acts as a bridle for the steed;
indeed, the yogi must always remain focused on the practice of sound.
Bound and freed from flickering through the digestion of the mercury of the mind with the sulfur of the *nāda*, it attains flight in the sky known as the supportless.
By hearing the inner sound (nāda), one quickly forgets all internal serpents; being single-pointed, one no longer runs after anything whatsoever.
Fire set ablaze in wood is extinguished along with the wood;
the mind set in motion by the *nāda* dissolves along with the *nāda*.
For one whose inner mind-deer is distracted and fixed upon the sound of bells and such,
even striking it down would be easy, provided one is skilled in aiming the arrow.
The resonance of the unstruck sound (*anāhata*) which is perceived, within that resonance is the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), and within the object of knowledge is the mind (*manas*).
Therein the mind attains dissolution; that is the supreme state of Viṣṇu.
As long as sound proceeds, there is the conceptualization of space;
that which is beyond sound is the Supreme Brahman, celebrated as the Paramātman.
Whatever is heard in the form of sound is indeed Śakti;
that which is at the end of the principles (tattvas), formless, is the Supreme Lord himself.
Thus is the contemplation of the *nāda*;
all these means of *haṭha* and *laya* yoga are for the sake of attaining *rājayoga*.
A person who has ascended to *rājayoga* is a deceiver of time.
Reality is the seed, Haṭha is the field, and equanimity is the water; by these three, the wish-fulfilling creeper of the Transmental state immediately springs forth.
Through constant pursuit of the inner sound (nāda), the accumulations of sin are destroyed;
the mind and the vital breath certainly dissolve into the stainless state. (HYP 4.105)
One never hears the sound of conchs or drums; by means of the state of *unmanī*, the body certainly becomes like a piece of wood. (HYP 4.106)
Freed from all states and devoid of all thought, the yogi remains like one who is dead; he is liberated—of this there is no doubt.
The yogi who is joined with meditative absorption is not devoured by time, is not afflicted by karma, and cannot be overcome by anyone. (HYP 4.108)
The yogi, disciplined in meditative absorption, perceives neither smell nor taste, neither form nor touch, nor sound; he perceives neither self nor other. (HYP 4.109)
He whose mind is neither asleep nor waking, who is free from both mindfulness and forgetfulness,
and which neither sets nor rises— he is indeed liberated.
The yogi who is disciplined in meditative absorption does not perceive cold or heat, nor likewise pain or pleasure; he has neither pride nor comparison.
He who remains established in his own true nature while awake, as if asleep,
and is free from inhalation and exhalation— he is certainly liberated.
The yogi who is disciplined in meditative absorption is invulnerable to all weapons, cannot be overcome by any embodied beings, and cannot be seized by mantras or yantras. (HYP 4.113)
As long as the vital wind (māruta), moving through the central path, does not enter [the central channel],
as long as one does not become firm through the binding of the life-force wind (prāṇavāta),
and as long as the reality (tattva) resembling the innate (sahaja) does not arise in meditative absorption (dhyāna).
To speak of knowledge at such a time is merely hypocrisy and false prattle.
Thus ends the fourth instruction, titled "The Characteristics of Samādhi," in the Haṭhayoga-pradīpikā.
